title: With me?
description:
Do you understand?
/wɪð miː/
widh MEE
details:
“Are you with me?” means “Do you understand what I’m explaining?” “You with me?” is an informal version.

Example: “Are you with me?”

title: Flat out
description:
Extremely busy.
/ˌflæt ˈaʊt/
flat OUT
details:
“Flat out” means extremely busy.

Usage: “I’m flat out with work today.”

Example: “I’m flat out today.”

title: Rustle up
description:
Prepare food quickly.
/ˈrʌsəl ʌp/
RUSS-uhl UP
details:
“Rustle something up” means quickly prepare food.

Usage: “I’ll rustle up a quick lunch.”

Example: “I’ll rustle up lunch.”

title: In a rush
description:
Little time available.
/ɪn ə rʌʃ/
in uh RUSH
details:
“In a rush” and “in a hurry” mean having little time.

Usage: “I need something easy to cook when I’m in a rush.”

Example: “I’m in a rush.”

title: Not a single…
description:
Not even one.
/nɒt ə ˈsɪŋɡəl/
not uh SING-guhl
details:
“I can’t think of a single…” means I cannot think of even one example.

Usage: “I can’t think of a single reason.”

Example: “I can’t think of a single reason.”

title: Beat the eggs
description:
Mix whites and yolks.
/biːt ði eɡz/
beet thee EGZ
details:
“Beat the eggs” means mix the yolks and whites together quickly with a fork or whisk.

Example: “Beat the eggs with a fork.”

title: Omelette
description:
Egg filling in this roll.
/ˈɒmlət/
OM-luht
details:
In this recipe, “the omelette centre” means the egg filling inside the tortilla roll.

Example: “Put the omelette in the wrap.”

title: Tortilla
description:
Thin, round flatbread.
/tɔːˈtiːə/
taw-TEE-uh
details:
A tortilla is a thin, round flatbread that can wrap around food. This is the British pronunciation. American pronunciation: /tɔːrˈtiːjə/, tor-TEE-yuh.

Example: “Wrap it in a tortilla.”

title: Filling
description:
Food inside a wrap.
/ˈfɪlɪŋ/
FIL-ing
details:
“Filling” is the food inside a wrap or sandwich. Common fillings include chicken, beans, cheese, and vegetables.

Example: “Cheese is my favourite filling.”

title: Dried parsley
description:
Dried herb flakes.
/draɪd ˈpɑːsli/
dryd PAH-slee
details:
Dried parsley is a green herb dried into small flakes to flavour food. It keeps longer than fresh parsley.

Example: “Add some dried parsley.”

title: Garlic granules
description:
Small dried garlic bits.
/ˈɡɑːlɪk ˈɡrænjuːlz/
GAH-lik GRAN-yoolz
details:
Garlic granules are small pieces of dried garlic used to add flavour.

Example: “Add a pinch of garlic granules.”

title: Kitchen staples
description:
Basic food supplies.
/ˈkɪtʃən ˈsteɪpəlz/
KITCH-uhn STAY-puhlz
details:
“Store cupboard staples” are basic ingredients you regularly keep at home, such as rice, oil, and dried herbs.

Example: “Rice and oil are kitchen staples.”

title: Meaty texture
description:
Feels like meat.
/ˈmiːti ˈtekstʃə/
MEE-tee TEKS-chuh
details:
“Meaty texture” means something feels like meat when you eat it.

Usage: “These mushrooms have a meaty texture.”

Example: “These mushrooms have a meaty texture.”

title: Flexible
description:
Usable in many ways.
/ˈfleksəbəl/
FLEK-suh-buhl
details:
“A flexible ingredient” can be used in many different ways.

Usage: “Eggs are a flexible ingredient.”

Example: “Eggs are a flexible ingredient.”

title: Flavour boost
description:
An increase in flavour.
/ˈfleɪvə buːst/
FLAY-vuh BOOST
details:
“An instant flavour boost” means an immediate increase in flavour.

Usage: “Dried herbs give the eggs an instant flavour boost.”

Example: “Herbs give it a flavour boost.”

title: Presenter
description:
A programme’s host.
/prɪˈzentə/
pri-ZEN-tuh
details:
“Presenter” or “host” describes the person leading a programme or video.

Usage: “The presenter shows us how to make egg rolls.”

Example: “The presenter makes egg rolls.”

title: Pronouns
description:
Words replacing nouns.
/ˈprəʊnaʊnz/
PROH-nownz
details:
Pronouns are words such as “she” and “her.” “The presenter” is a noun phrase; “she” can replace it.

Example: “The presenter cooks. She beats the eggs.”

title: Present tense
description:
Use it for summaries.
/ˌprezənt ˈtens/
PREZ-uhnt TENS
details:
Video summaries often use present tense: “She beats three eggs.”

Past tense also works when recounting what you watched: “She beat three eggs.”

Example: “She beats three eggs.”

title: Salt and pepper
description:
No “s” on “pepper”.
/sɒlt ən ˈpepə/
solt uhn PEP-uh
details:
“Salt and pepper” is the usual phrase for the seasonings. Use “pepper” without an “s” here.

Example: “Add salt and pepper.”

title: Vocabulary
description:
Say “some vocabulary”.
/vəˈkæbjələri/
vuh-KAB-yuh-luh-ree
details:
“Vocabulary” is usually uncountable when discussing words you learn.

Say “I learned a few new words” or “I learned some new vocabulary.”

Example: “I learned some new vocabulary.”

title: Make a meal
description:
Prepare a meal.
/meɪk ə mɪəl/
mayk uh MIH-uhl
details:
“Make a meal” is the natural expression.

Usage: “She shows us how to make a quick meal.”

For “meal”, blend MIH-uhl into one syllable, with the vowel in British “near”.

Example: “Let’s make a quick meal.”

title: Call her?
description:
Ask for a name or role.
/kɔːl hə/
KAWL huh
details:
“What should I call her?” is a natural way to ask which name or role word to use for someone.

Example: “What should I call her?”

title: Common fillings
description:
What goes in a wrap?
/ˈkɒmən ˈfɪlɪŋz/
KOM-uhn FIL-ingz
details:
“What fillings do people usually use?” is a natural way to ask what normally goes inside a tortilla.

Example: “What fillings do people usually use?”

title: Even though
description:
Contrast: don’t add “but”.
/ˈiːvən ðəʊ/
EE-vuhn THOH
details:
“Even though” already expresses contrast, so leave out “but.”

Usage: “Even though I haven’t finished the video, I’m surprised by how easy the recipe looks.”

Example: “Even though it’s simple, it’s tasty.”

title: Summary
description:
Topic → details → view.
/ˈsʌməri/
SUM-uh-ree
details:
Explain what the video is about, mention two important points, then give your opinion if you want to.

Framework: topic → two key details → optional reaction.

Example: “She makes egg rolls. They’re quick and easy.”

title: Keep it short
description:
2–3 sentences can do.
/kiːp ɪt ʃɔːt/
keep it SHAWT
details:
A short clip only needs a short summary. Two or three sentences can be enough; you don’t need every ingredient or detail.

Example: “She makes egg rolls with a tortilla. It looks easy.”
